title: Shared Responsibility Model
summary: The shared responsibility model is the contractual and architectural division of security duties between a cloud service provider and its customer, in which the provider secures the cloud itself while the customer secures what they put in the cloud. The split is not uniform: for infrastructure as a service the provider owns the physical facilities, hosts, hypervisor and network fabric, while the customer owns the guest operating system, patching, identity, data and application; for platform as a service the provider absorbs the runtime and middleware, leaving the customer identity, configuration and data; for software as a service the provider operates nearly the whole stack and the customer retains responsibility for accounts, access grants, data classification and how the service is used. Security professionals rely on the model because most cloud incidents occur in the customer's portion of the stack, particularly identity misconfiguration, overly permissive policies, exposed storage and unpatched workloads. Applying it demands more than reading a marketing diagram: teams must map each control in their own framework to a named owner, record the evidence source, and confirm the split for every managed service they adopt, since the boundary shifts service by service and even feature by feature. Auditors expect this mapping to be documented and traceable, and incident responders need it to know who to contact and what telemetry the provider will and will not expose.
objectives: You will be able to explain how responsibility shifts across IaaS, PaaS and SaaS and why the boundary differs per managed service.
You will be able to map a control framework to provider and customer ownership and identify which side supplies the evidence.
You will be able to recognise the misconfiguration classes that repeatedly fall on the customer side of the line.
You will be able to use provider documentation to settle disputed ownership during an incident or audit.
You will be able to brief engineering and procurement teams on the security work they still own after adoption.
